newsitem.title: USA: House Republicans face tough fight in California.
newsitem.headline: House Republicans face tough fight in California.

text.p: Several Republican members of Congress are fighting for their political lives in California, a state that could sway the balance as Democrats try to regain control of the House of Representatives.

Reps. Robert Dornan of Orange County, Bill Baker of the San Francisco Bay area, Frank Riggs of the north coast, and Brian Bilbray of San Diego are among the Republicans whose seats may be in play on Nov. 5, political analysts said.

In 1994, Republicans won control of both houses for the first time in four decades. Republicans currently hold a 235-197 majority in the House of Representatives. But many of those who swept into office as part of the 1994 Republican tide are now vulnerable.
"A theme is emerging," said Bruce Cain, professor of political science at the University of California at Berkeley. "The Republicans took the revolution too far. They're battling for their lives."

Political analysts are divided on how President Clinton's lead will influence California's congressional races. Analysts said some Democrats could be elected on Clinton's coattails, but recent polls suggest a growing number of voters do not want to see a Democratic Congress if Clinton is re-elected.

Likewise, while Dole's focus on the hot-button issues of immigration and affirmative action could bring conservative voters out on election day, minority voters in the state could mobilise against Republican candidates, analysts said.
The ultra-conservative and flamboyant Robert "B-1 Bob" Dornan from the heart of Orange County is one of several Republicans who could be unseated, analysts said.
Dornan, who has been in Congress for 18 years, is facing well-funded Democratic businesswoman Loretta Sanchez, who is Hispanic. Recent polls point to a close race.
"I make every race a tight race in my mind, looking over my shoulder at all times," said Dornan, a former fighter pilot. "I'm going to peak on election day."

The race is not only a test of Dornan's staying power following his failed bid for the Republican presidential nomination earlier this year. Analysts said the race will also test the growing electoral clout of Hispanics in his district.

"In the wake of welfare reform and the rhetoric on immigration reform, Latinos have been registering more, and registering more Democratic," said Sherry Bebitch Jeffe, a political analyst at California's Claremont Graduate School. "The (Republican) immigrant bashing may backfire on Dornan."
Turnout by Latinos on election day could be the deciding factor in this race, political analysts said.

"The Latino vote is ... going to be more significant than it's ever been in the past," said Sanchez. "With the immigrant bashing that's been going on, the Hispanic community has figured out that it's about time to stand up and say 'No.'"

In the San Francisco Bay area, which has few Republican enclaves, Democratic House candidate Ellen Tauscher threatens to unseat incumbent Baker, analysts said. She has run an aggressive campaign, accusing Baker of receiving hundreds of thousands of dollars in campaign contributions from tobacco firms and the gun lobby.
Baker, running for a third term, has shot back by accusing Tauscher of trying to buy the election.
In several other key races, Democrats are pouring millions of dollars into ads painting their Republican opponents as beholden to unpopular House Speaker Newt Gingrich.

"I have not heard of one Republican in California sending out mailers with pictures of Newt Gingrich," said Bob Mulholland, campaign adviser for the California Democratic Party. "Meanwhile, we've sent out millions of them."

Along California's north coast, Democrat Michela Alioto, the 28-year-old granddaughter of former San Francisco Mayor Joe Alioto, is running a tight race against Republican incumbent Riggs. In her ads, she has tried to link her opponent to Gingrich and the Christian Coalition.

William Lammers, a professor of political science at the University of Southern California, said Riggs could lose his seat. "Alioto seems to be a rather attractive campaigner, albeit young," he said. "Riggs is in trouble."
Meanwhile, in San Diego, Bilbray is facing a brash challenger in Peter Navarro, who has made Gingrich the centrepiece of his campaign, dubbing his rival "Newt Bilbray."

A vocal backer of the Contract with America two years ago, Bilbray now paints himself as independent. "Brian Bilbray is no Newt Gingrich," said Bilbray campaign manager Steve Danon. "He represents the people, not necessarily the party."
